common_name: Wakehurst Pieris (AGM Brilliant Red New-Growth Himalayan Andromeda)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade sheltered from early morning sun and cold wind; Wakehurst's tender spring flush is vulnerable to late frost damage, so choose a protected site.

directions: Wakehurst is the most celebrated form of the Chinese and Himalayan species Pieris formosa var. forrestii, prized above all for a spring flush of brilliant scarlet-red new growth that fades through crimson-pink before settling into green, a display many consider the finest of any hardy Pieris. Named for Wakehurst Place in Sussex, where it was exhibited by Gerald Loder and awarded a First Class Certificate in 1930, it also carries large, freely borne trusses of white, urn-shaped flowers in spring. It grows into a substantial, eventually tree-like shrub in favorable gardens, but the tender new growth is easily damaged by late spring frosts, so a sheltered site helps protect the color show. Give it the same acidic, humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil favored by rhododendrons, with room to develop its considerable eventual size.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Jermyns holds decorative pink flower buds through the winter months well before they open, adding cold-season interest ahead of bloom.

directions: Jermyns takes its name from Jermyns House in Hampshire, home of the Hillier family, and earned a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Merit in 1959 for its long season of interest. Its flower buds form a distinct pink well before winter's end, giving the shrub a softly colored presence through the coldest months, long before the white, urn-shaped flowers finally open in spring. Like other forms of Pieris formosa var. forrestii it also produces a colorful flush of new spring growth, though the pink winter buds are its signature feature. Acidic, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture and shelter from harsh winter wind and late frost keep it performing at its best.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Charles Michael Pieris (Bronze New-Growth Caerhays Andromeda)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade in a site sheltered from harsh wind; Charles Michael comes from the mild Cornish garden at Caerhays and appreciates similarly protected conditions elsewhere.

directions: Charles Michael is a Cornish selection derived from plants growing at Caerhays Castle, honored with a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Merit in 1965. Its new spring growth emerges a warm bronze rather than the fiery scarlet of 'Wakehurst', giving a softer, more subdued seasonal color change before the foliage matures to glossy green. Upright, well-filled panicles of white, urn-shaped flowers follow in spring, held clear of the foliage. As with other forms of Pieris formosa var. forrestii, it needs acidic, humus-rich, consistently moist soil and benefits from the same sheltered, mild conditions as its Cornish origin, so protect it from harsh winter wind and late frosts in colder gardens.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

common_name: Balls of Fire Pieris (Bright Red New-Growth Irish-Raised Andromeda)
scientific_name: Pieris formosa var. forrestii 'Balls of Fire'

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade with shelter from cold wind and late frost; Balls of Fire hails from an exceptionally mild Irish garden and is less forgiving of harsh winters than many pieris.

directions: Balls of Fire was raised at Fota Arboretum in County Cork, Ireland, a garden renowned for testing tender and unusual woody plants in its exceptionally mild microclimate. It was selected for young foliage that emerges a vivid, saturated red, rivaling 'Wakehurst' for intensity of spring color before the leaves mature to green. White, urn-shaped flowers appear in spring in the same manner as other Pieris formosa var. forrestii selections. Because it originated in one of the mildest gardens in the British Isles, give it a sheltered, frost-protected site with acidic, humus-rich soil in regions prone to hard late frosts.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Rowallane Pieris (Yellow New-Growth Seedling of Wakehurst)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade with shelter from cold wind and late frost, as for other Pieris formosa var. forrestii selections.

directions: Rowallane arose as a self-sown seedling of 'Wakehurst' at Rowallane Garden in County Down, Northern Ireland, now cared for by the National Trust. Rather than repeating its parent's fiery red, its new spring growth unfurls a clear, unusual yellow before greening up, giving it a distinct place among the colorful new-growth forms of Pieris formosa var. forrestii. Clusters of white, urn-shaped spring flowers follow in the same manner as its relatives. It shares the same cultural needs as other var. forrestii selections, wanting acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil and shelter from cold wind and late frost to protect the developing spring foliage.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Elongata is considerably more cold-hardy than Asian Pieris japonica selections and tolerates more sun in cooler climates.

directions: Elongata is a long-recognized selection of the Appalachian native mountain fetterbush, distinguished from the typical species by upright flower racemes that can stretch to twice the usual length, sometimes reaching eight inches. It was raised at the English Keeper's Hill Nursery and received a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Merit in 1938 for the unusually showy effect of its extended white, urn-shaped flower spikes in spring. Like the species, it forms a dense, rounded, cold-hardy evergreen shrub considerably tougher in winter than Asian Pieris japonica, and its upright rather than drooping flower clusters give it a distinct silhouette in bloom. Acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil and a site sheltered from harsh winter sun and wind suit it best, as with all pieris.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Daisen Pieris (Deep Pink Bud, Mountain-Collected Japanese Andromeda)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Daisen was the parent selection from which 'Christmas Cheer' arose and shares its rich pink bud color.

directions: Daisen was collected on Mount Daisen in western Japan and is valued for flower buds that open a deep, saturated pink before gradually paling as the urn-shaped blossoms mature and fully expand. It served as the parent plant from which the popular early-flowering 'Christmas Cheer' arose as a garden seedling, and it shares that cultivar's rich bud color while typically flowering at a more conventional spring timing. Plants build a well-proportioned, moderately compact evergreen habit with the glossy foliage typical of the species. Consistent moisture in acidic, humus-rich soil and a partially shaded site sheltered from harsh winter wind and sun bring out the richest bud color and the healthiest foliage.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Rosalinda's compact four-foot habit fits foundation plantings and smaller borders better than larger pieris cultivars.

directions: Rosalinda is a compact Dutch-trialed selection that reaches only about four feet, considerably smaller than many pink-flowered pieris cultivars, making it easier to fit into foundation plantings and smaller shrub borders. Its pink flowers open from contrasting brown buds, and glossy dark-green leaves emerge with a brownish-red flush that fades to green as the foliage matures through the season. It scored well in the long-running Boskoop cultivar trials in the Netherlands, reflecting reliable garden performance and a dense, tidy habit. Give it the same acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil and partial shade that all Japanese andromeda selections need, with shelter from harsh winter wind and sun.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Blush Pieris (Rosy Pink Fading Open-Habit Andromeda)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Blush grows in a looser, more open habit than many compact modern pieris cultivars, so allow it room to arch.

directions: Blush was first exhibited in 1967 and is valued for an open, elegant habit that reaches about five feet, giving it a looser silhouette than many densely mounded modern pieris cultivars. Its urn-shaped flowers open a clear rosy pink and gradually pale with age, extending the color display over several weeks rather than fading all at once. Clean evergreen foliage and a naturally graceful branching pattern make it useful as an accent among more tightly mounded shrubs in a mixed border. As with other Japanese andromeda selections, it needs acidic, humus-rich, consistently moist soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh winter sun and wind.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
